name: Hundred Days' Reform
info: The Hundred Days' Reform, or Wuxu Reform, was a short-lived reform movement in the Qing Empire from 11 June to 21 September 1898, in which the Guangxu Emperor and scholars such as Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao sought to modernise China's institutions.

facts.where: the Qing Empire, with the court at Beijing; Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao fled afterwards to Japan
facts.period: from 11 June to 21 September 1898, roughly 100 days; ended by the coup of Empress Dowager Cixi in September 1898
facts.figures: the Guangxu Emperor, who initiated it; Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao, the reformers who led it; Tan Sitong, a reformist thinker; Empress Dowager Cixi, who ended it; Yuan Shikai and Ronglu, whose forces supported the coup
facts.outcome: most measures faced resistance, and the coup of September 1898 put the emperor under house arrest and ended the programme; the Imperial University of Peking, now Peking University, survived, and later Qing reforms followed after 1901

t: The reform was a response to China's defeat by Meiji Japan in the First Sino-Japanese War (1894–1895), which Chinese elites took as evidence that the Self-Strengthening Movement's focus on weapons and machinery had failed.

Over roughly 100 days the Guangxu Emperor issued edicts on education, administration, the economy and the military, among them the founding of the Imperial University of Peking, but most measures met resistance from conservatives.
Empress Dowager Cixi ended the programme with a coup in September 1898, placed the emperor under house arrest and had the leading reformers ordered executed; she later backed the late Qing reforms.
dyk: The Imperial University of Peking, set up during the Hundred Days' Reform, is now Peking University. Guangxu, put under house arrest on Yingtai Island after the coup, remained there until his death in 1908.
ev: The First Opium War begins, the first of two defeats that started China's effort to modernise
The Jiangnan Arsenal is established in Shanghai and becomes the largest factory in China
The First Sino-Japanese War begins; China is defeated by Meiji Japan in 1895, and the Treaty of Shimonoseki cedes Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula
The Guangxu Emperor begins to issue the reform edicts, on 11 June
Empress Dowager Cixi stages a coup, places the emperor under house arrest and orders the leading reformers executed
The imperial examination is abolished, one of the late Qing reforms that followed
The Xinhai Revolution succeeds, a result to which the failure of the late Qing reforms contributed

sections.background:
After its defeat in the First (1839–1842) and Second (1856–1860) Opium Wars, China began an effort to modernise that became the Self-Strengthening Movement. Military modernisation was a high priority from the start, and the movement concentrated more on supplying the armed forces with modern weapons than on reforming governance or society. Li Hongzhang and others wanted a modernised military that joined western innovations to China, and they and a majority believed that through western influence China could strengthen its economy and protect itself on a global stage. The British military had flintlocks, caplocks and breech-loading rifled artillery, while the Qing had matchlock muskets with far fewer rounds and lower accuracy.

China also wished to improve its own weapon manufacturing by building more domestic factories. The Jiangnan Arsenal, established in Shanghai in 1865, was the largest factory in China and produced ships, breech-loading rifles and artillery shells. Even so, it was considered underdeveloped beside Europe's, and it was deprived of imperial funding. The military lacked the organisation, training and institutions needed to sustain coming wars.

The First Sino-Japanese War (1894–1895), in which Qing China was defeated by Meiji Japan, a state that had undergone more comprehensive reforms in the same period, exposed these limits. The Treaty of Shimonoseki forced China to recognise Korean independence, cede Taiwan and the Liaodong Peninsula and pay a large indemnity. Chinese elites viewed the defeat as clear evidence that the Self-Strengthening Movement had failed and as a sign that institutional and constitutional change was required.
sections.aims:
Reformist thinkers such as Tan Sitong, Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao responded to what they saw as China's deep crisis, which included political division, insurrection, opium addiction and growing foreign conflicts. They worked through memorials to the throne, reform and study societies and widely circulated political essays. Influenced by the success of Japan's Meiji constitutional reforms, they argued that China needed change to its governing institutions, its educational systems and its social order, not only better armies and arsenals.

The proposals covered several fields. In education they included Peking University, where the sciences, liberal arts and Chinese classics were to be studied together, a modern system teaching mathematics and science rather than mainly Confucian texts, a gradual replacement of the civil service examination curriculum and study abroad for members of the imperial family. In government they included a transition to a constitutional monarchy on the Meiji model, with deliberative institutions and limits on autocratic rule, and the abolition of the traditional examination system, which reformers saw as an obstacle to a modern bureaucracy and to social mobility.

In the economy they proposed ending sinecures, encouraging joint stock enterprises and private investment, founding trade schools and creating a bureau for railways and mines, with agricultural schools in every province. In the military they proposed Western-style training, drilling and staff systems, a modern military academy and a modern naval academy.
sections.events:
Elements of the Qing government were alarmed enough to permit Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao to put reforms to the Guangxu Emperor, who agreed and committed himself to the programme. From 11 June to 21 September 1898 the throne issued a rapid series of edicts on education, administration, the economy and the military. Some measures were carried out, such as the founding of the Imperial University of Peking, but most met resistance.

Opposition among the conservative ruling elite was intense. They condemned the reforms as too radical and proposed more moderate, gradual alternatives. Senior Manchu princes, Grand Councilors and provincial governors resisted, many of them viewing the revision of the examination system and the abolition of sinecures as direct threats to the existing order. Conservatives feared that foreign advisers and Japanese models would place the Qing state under foreign influence, and Prince Duan urged the expulsion of Timothy Richard and the former prime minister Itō Hirobumi from the court. Empress Dowager Cixi supported the principles of the reform, but feared that sudden implementation without bureaucratic support would be disruptive and that Japan and other foreign powers would exploit any weakness.

As tensions between the emperor and Cixi grew, some reformers plotted to remove her by force. According to later accounts, Tan Sitong asked Yuan Shikai to kill Ronglu, take control of the garrison at Tientsin and march on Beijing to arrest Cixi. Yuan had earlier promised to support Ronglu and told him of the plot, which let Cixi and her faction prepare a coup d'état. With the support of the conservatives and the armed forces commanded by Yuan and Ronglu, Cixi took over the government in September 1898.
sections.people:
The Guangxu Emperor initiated the reform. According to Sterling Seagrave, he bypassed the Grand Council and appointed four reformers to advise him after a series of interviews, in which Kang Youwei was rejected. He also held secret talks with the former Japanese prime minister Itō Hirobumi, hoping to use his experience of the Meiji Restoration. Guangxu was put under house arrest on Yingtai Island until his death in 1908.

Kang Youwei and his student Liang Qichao were the two principal leaders, scholars who proposed the reforms to the emperor. Tan Sitong, a reformist thinker, refused to flee after the coup and was executed. The "Six Gentlemen of Wuxu" were Tan Sitong, Kang Guangren (Kang Youwei's brother), Lin Xu, Yang Shenxiu, Yang Rui and Liu Guangdi. Students of Kang and Liang formed the Kang Party, which was one of the groups that most alarmed court conservatives.

On the other side stood Empress Dowager Cixi, with allies among the conservative elite, and the armed forces of Yuan Shikai and Ronglu. The generals Dong Fuxiang, Ma Anliang and Ma Haiyan were called to Beijing and helped end the movement, along with Ma Fulu and Ma Fuxiang. Dong Fuxiang and the Muslim Gansu Army stationed in Beijing later took part in the Boxer Rebellion and became known as the Kansu Braves. The British missionary Timothy Richard, whom Kang invited to Beijing, also figures in the events of September 1898.
sections.outcomes:
The coup reversed the reforms. The old writing style was put back into mandate, the offices and agencies that had been removed were reinstituted, and the establishment of certain newspapers, civil societies and schools was suspended. The chief advocates, the Six Gentlemen of Wuxu, were ordered to be executed. Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao fled to Japan, where they founded the Baohuang Hui (Protect the Emperor Society) and worked, unsuccessfully, for a constitutional monarchy in China.

An alternative view holds that Kang and Liang had a different aim in leaving for Japan: not only to justify fleeing China but also to solicit intervention by foreign powers such as Britain or Japan to rescue the emperor.

The late Qing reforms after 1901 included the abolition of the imperial examination in 1905, educational and military modernisation patterned on Japan, and experiments in constitutional and parliamentary government. Their ultimate failure gave impetus to revolutionary forces: changes within the establishment came to be seen as largely hopeless, and the overthrow of the Qing increasingly appeared the only way to save China. Such sentiments directly contributed to the success of the Xinhai Revolution in 1911.
sections.legacy:
Although brief, the movement introduced new political concepts of nationhood and sovereignty, and it inspired many of the "New Policies" reforms launched after 1901. Cixi herself backed the late Qing reforms after the invasions of the Eight-Nation Alliance. The Imperial University of Peking, founded in the movement, is now Peking University.

Historians differ over the failure. The mainstream view is that the reformers were heroic but unorganised, trying to reform and save a backward state but hampered by the ruling conservative faction led by Cixi, who feared the results would impede their own power. Some historians of the late 20th century take a view more favourable to the conservatives and less to the reformers: that Kang Youwei and his allies were hopeless dreamers unaware of the political realities, and that the conservative elites were not opposed to change. Sterling Seagrave, in The Dragon Lady, argues that Manchu nobles of the xenophobic iron hats faction dominated the Grand Council, and that Kang had far less influence than his later boasting suggested. It has also been suggested, controversially, that Kang's perceived arrogance harmed the cause and that false rumours reached the Grand Council.

Professor Lei Chia-sheng argues that Timothy Richard's plan of 18 September, in which China would join a federation of ten nations, convinced Cixi to end the reforms with the coup. Leo Tolstoy corresponded with Gu Hongming on the reform and agreed that it was ill-advised.

summary: The Hundred Days' Reform was a movement in the Qing Empire from 11 June to 21 September 1898, led by the Guangxu Emperor with Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao, which sought to modernise China's institutions after defeat by Japan. Empress Dowager Cixi ended it with a coup, and the leading reformers were ordered executed.
references: Rebecca E. Karl, Rethinking the 1898 Reform Period: Political and Cultural Change in Late Qing China ((Harvard UP, 2002)
Luke S. K. Kwong, A Mosaic of the Hundred Days: Personalities, Politics, and Ideas of 1898 (Harvard University Press, 1984)
notes: Dates: the lede says the reform ran from 11 June to 21 September 1898 and that Cixi staged the coup on 21 September; the section 'Cixi ends the program' says 22 September. I gave only 'September 1898' for the coup. start and end are both 1898.
The lede says Cixi executed six leading reformers; the section says they were 'ordered to be executed' and names Tan Sitong as executed. I wrote 'ordered executed' and said only Tan was executed.
Left out: the article's statement that Cixi conducted reforms after the Taiping Rebellion 'in 1850' (the Tongzhi Restoration), since the date looks garbled.
Left out the Kansu Braves detail beyond the one sentence, and the See also list.

The Seagrave and Lei Chia-sheng views are attributed as the article gives them; the 'Failure as Kang's responsibility' section also says Kang 'perceived arrogance' as a controversial suggestion, kept as such.
The people section gives Guangxu's bypassing of the Grand Council and talks with Itō as Seagrave's account.
Key events 1839–1842 and 1865 are background events; the article has no dated events inside the 100 days except the start date and the coup.
